query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles with near‐equiatomic multi-element mixing that minimizes atomic size mismatch and incorporates a buffering element (e.g., an oxygen sublattice in oxides) exhibit enhanced structural and chemical stability at high temperatures because lattice distortion increases diffusion barriers and the buffer layer relieves local stresses, thereby inhibiting phase separation and surface segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles synthesized by physical or chemical routes with a uniform elemental distribution and minimal atomic size mismatch; in oxide systems, an oxygen sublattice is present.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the nanoparticle composition by (a) introducing or removing a buffering element (e.g., oxygen) and (b) substituting one or more constituents to increase the atomic size mismatch.
generation.conditions: High-temperature catalytic conditions (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric conditions (473–1923 K) under atmospheres relevant to their applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion induced by near‐equiatomic mixing coupled with the presence of a buffering sublattice that accommodates local strain.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of a near‐equiatomic mixture promotes a single solid‐solution phase; concomitant lattice distortions elevate the energy barriers for atomic diffusion and segregation, and a buffering element (such as oxygen in an oxide) relieves local mechanical stresses, collectively hindering phase separation and degradation during service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with minimal atomic size mismatch and a buffering element will display essentially unchanged single-phase solid-solution structures and uniform composition after high-temperature exposure, whereas those with increased size mismatch or lacking the buffer will show signs of phase separation, elemental segregation, or secondary phase formation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced under standard near‐equiatomic conditions with low atomic size mismatch and with the buffering element present are expected to maintain their structure under the set conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles where the key factors are atomic size compatibility and the presence of a buffering component; it may not hold if the size mismatch exceeds a critical threshold or if additional degradation mechanisms (e.g., surface oxidation under certain atmospheres) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical values of atomic size mismatch and the quantitative contribution of the buffering layer to stability remain to be determined; interactions with specific operating atmospheres (e.g., oxidizing vs inert) may also introduce variability in the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set following the baseline synthesis with near‐equiatomic composition, minimal size mismatch, and a buffering component (e.g., oxygen-doped oxide), and a second set in which the atomic size mismatch is intentionally increased (via substitution with larger or smaller elements) and/or the buffering element is omitted. Subject both sets to high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and/or thermoelectric (473–1923 K) environments for a fixed period.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect phase separation or the emergence of secondary phases.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for nanoscale morphological changes and elemental mapping.
Surface compositional analysis (e.g., X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) to assess elemental segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the baseline nanoparticles (with low atomic size mismatch and buffering element) exhibit similar or higher degrees of phase separation, elemental segregation, or structural degradation under identical high-temperature conditions than the intentionally destabilized nanoparticles, then the proposed role of lattice distortion and buffering in ensuring high-temperature stability is falsified.

(Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Highly efficient decomposition of ammonia using high-entropy alloy catalysts

Abstract: Ammonia represents a promising liquid fuel for hydrogen storage, but its large-scale application is limited by the need for precious metal ruthenium (Ru) as catalyst. Here we report on highly efficient ammonia decomposition using novel high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalysts made of earth abundant elements. Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram. These HEA nanoparticles demonstrate substantially enhanced catalytic activity and stability for ammonia decomposition, with improvement factors achieving >20 versus Ru catalysts. Catalytic activity of HEA nanoparticles is robustly tunable by varying the Co/Mo ratio, allowing for the optimization of surface property to maximize the reactivity under different reaction conditions. High Entropy Alloys Mined From Binary Phase Diagrams

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are a new type of high-performance structural material. Their vast degrees of compositional freedom provide for extensive opportunities to design alloys with tailored properties. However, compositional complexities present challenges for alloy design. Current approaches have shown limited reliability in accounting for the compositional regions of single solid solution and composite phases. For the first time, a phenomenological method analysing binary phase diagrams to predict HEA phases is presented. The hypothesis is that the HEA structural stability is encoded within the phase diagrams. Accordingly, we introduce several phase-diagram inspired parameters and employ machine learning (ML) to classify 600+ reported HEAs based on these parameters. Compared to other large database statistical prediction models, this model gives more detailed and accurate phase predictions. Both the overall HEA prediction and specifically single-phase HEA prediction rate are above 80%.
